faq.a: Yes; low titres (≤1:40) are common, especially in the elderly, and are usually clinically insignificant.
faq.q: Can a healthy person have a positive ANA?

faq.a: Acute malaria can cause transient false‑positive ANA, so interpretation must consider recent infection.
faq.q: Why is ANA less useful in malaria‑endemic areas?

faq.a: Assess for infection first; if infection is excluded, evaluate for systemic autoimmune disease with specific antibody panels.
faq.q: What is the next step after a positive ANA in a febrile patient?

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with joint pain, photosensitivity, and a 1:320 ANA – what further tests confirm SLE? — Order anti‑dsDNA and complement; high anti‑dsDNA and low C3/C4 support active SLE.
A patient on long‑term hydralazine develops a rash and a 1:160 ANA – how do you differentiate drug‑induced lupus? — Consider drug history, lack of anti‑dsDNA, and resolution after drug withdrawal.

In a rural clinic without IIF, a patient has a strong clinical suspicion of SLE but ANA is unavailable – what is your management? — Base treatment on clinical criteria, start low‑dose steroids, arrange referral for confirmatory testing.

A child with fever, anemia, and a 1:80 ANA from a malaria‑endemic area – what is the most likely explanation? — Malaria can cause transient low‑titre ANA; treat malaria first and repeat ANA after recovery.
How does the ANA pattern guide you toward systemic sclerosis versus SLE? — Nucleolar pattern points to systemic sclerosis; homogeneous or speckled patterns suggest SLE.

A patient with lupus nephritis has rising anti‑dsDNA titres – what does this indicate? — Increasing titres correlate with worsening renal disease; intensify immunosuppression and monitor renal function.
Why should you avoid high‑dose steroids in a patient with active TB and positive ANA? — Steroids can exacerbate TB; treat TB first and use steroid-sparing agents if autoimmune disease is confirmed.
What warning signs in an ANA‑positive patient require urgent referral? — New neurologic deficits, rapidly rising creatinine, or severe cytopenias demand immediate specialist input.
ai.title: Antinuclear Antibody (ANA) Testing
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: ANA detects auto‑antibodies against nuclear components, guiding diagnosis of systemic autoimmune diseases. Interpretation requires pattern recognition, titres, and clinical correlation, especially where resources are limited.

b: Screening tool for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and related disorders
Often the first serologic test ordered when multisystem symptoms are present
sections.p: ANA is an immunofluorescence or ELISA test that identifies antibodies directed against cellular nuclei. A positive result suggests systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease but can be seen in infections and healthy individuals.

t.b: Is the patient likely to have an autoimmune disease? – Positive at ≥1:80 (screening) suggests autoimmunity; higher titres increase specificity.
Which autoantibody is present? – Identifies anti‑dsDNA, anti‑Sm, anti‑RNP, etc., to refine diagnosis.

b: Speckled pattern → SLE, mixed connective tissue disease, Sjögren’s
Centromere pattern → limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis
sections.p: Interpretation hinges on titre, pattern, and clinical context. Common patterns (homogeneous, speckled, nucleolar, centromere) point to different diseases.

t.b: How strong is the antibody response? – Titres ≥1:160 in a symptomatic patient are more predictive of disease.

b: Rule out infection (TB, HIV, malaria) before immunosuppression
Consider drug‑induced lupus in patients on hydralazine, procainamide, or isoniazid
sections.p: Positive ANA guides further specific antibody testing and informs prognosis, especially in SLE where anti‑dsDNA correlates with renal involvement.

t.b: Is renal disease likely? – High titres correlate with lupus nephritis activity.
Is disease activity high? – Low complement suggests active SLE.

b: Always correlate a positive ANA with clinical features before labeling SLE
In low‑resource settings, a high‑titre ANA may be used as a provisional diagnosis when specific antibody tests are unavailable
sections.p: Examiners test your ability to integrate ANA results with history, exam, and resource constraints.

t.a: Bedside skin exam for malar rash, discoid lesions, photosensitivity
t.b: Does the patient meet clinical criteria for SLE? – Presence of ≥4 ACR/EULAR criteria supports diagnosis.

b: Assuming any positive ANA equals SLE
Ignoring infections or drug exposure that can cause false‑positive ANA
sections.p: Misinterpretation of low‑titre ANA or reliance on a single positive result leads to over‑diagnosis.

t.b: What to do? – Rely on clinical criteria and consider alternative serology (e.g., rheumatoid factor, CRP) while arranging referral.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly progressive renal failure, seizures, or severe cytopenias in a patient with positive ANA – urgent rheumatology input
